title: No. 35 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Before examining other objections to giving the Union an unlimited power of taxation, I want to make one general point. If the national government's authority over revenue were restricted to specific items, the burden of public taxes would inevitably fall too heavily on those items. Two evils would follow: certain industries would be oppressed, and taxes would be unequally distributed both among the states and among the citizens within each state.

Suppose, as some have argued, that the federal taxing power were limited to import duties. The government, unable to draw on other resources, would frequently be tempted to push these duties to harmful extremes. Some imagine such duties can never be too high. They argue that the higher the duties, the more they discourage extravagant consumption, encourage a favorable balance of trade, and promote domestic manufactures. But all extremes are harmful. Excessive duties on imports would breed widespread smuggling, which always hurts honest traders and eventually the revenue itself. They tax other classes of the community to benefit the manufacturing class by giving manufacturers a premature monopoly. They sometimes force industry out of its natural channels into less productive ones. Finally, they oppress the merchant, who must often pay them himself without recovering the cost from the consumer. When demand equals the supply at market, the consumer generally pays the duty. But when the markets are overstocked, much of the duty falls on the merchant, sometimes wiping out his profits and even cutting into his capital. I suspect the duty is shared between seller and buyer more often than people realize. It isn't always possible to raise the price of goods in exact proportion to every additional tax. The merchant, especially in a country with little commercial capital, is often forced to keep prices low to sell quickly.

It is far more often true that the consumer pays the duty than that the seller does. So it is more equitable for import duties to enter a common stock than to benefit only the importing states. But this isn't universally true enough to justify making such duties the only national fund. When the merchant pays them, they act as an extra tax on the importing state, whose citizens still pay their share as consumers. Viewed this way, they create inequality among the states, an inequality that grows with the size of the duties. Limiting national revenue to imports would also create inequality between manufacturing and non-manufacturing states. States that can supply more of their own needs through domestic manufactures will consume a smaller proportion of imports relative to their population or wealth. So they would not contribute to the public treasury in proportion to their ability. To make them do so requires resorting to excise taxes, which properly target specific kinds of manufactures. New York is more deeply affected by this than those of her citizens who want to limit the Union's taxing power to external duties may realize. New York is an importing state and unlikely to soon become a major manufacturing state. She would suffer doubly from confining the Union's authority to commercial duties.

As far as these observations suggest a danger that import duties might be pushed to harmful extremes, I have noted elsewhere that the interest of the revenue itself would be enough to prevent this. I admit this would hold true as long as other resources remained available. But if those avenues were closed, hope, driven by necessity, would produce experiments backed by strict precautions and additional penalties. These would, for a time, achieve the intended effect, until clever evasions could be devised. The first success would inspire false beliefs that long experience might be needed to correct. Necessity, especially in politics, often produces false hopes, false reasoning, and a corresponding system of mistaken measures. But even if no such excess resulted from limiting the federal taxing power, the inequalities I have mentioned would still occur, though to a lesser degree, from the other causes. Let us return to examining the objections.

One objection, judging by how often it is repeated, seems most relied on. It is that the House of Representatives is not numerous enough to include all the different classes of citizens, and so cannot combine the interests and feelings of every part of the community or produce a proper sympathy between representatives and their constituents. The argument has a plausible and seductive form, well calculated to appeal to the prejudices of those it addresses. But when carefully examined, it turns out to be made up of nothing but fine-sounding words. The aim it appears to seek is, first of all, impractical. And in the sense in which it is argued, it is unnecessary. I will discuss elsewhere whether the representative body has enough members. Here I will limit myself to examining the particular use that has been made of the contrary assumption regarding our subject.

The idea that every class should literally be represented by people from that same class is entirely unrealistic. Unless the Constitution required each occupation to send one or more members, it would never happen in practice. Mechanics and manufacturers will, with few exceptions, vote for merchants rather than people from their own trades. These discerning citizens know that mechanical and manufacturing arts supply the materials of mercantile enterprise. Many of them are directly tied to commerce. They know the merchant is their natural patron and friend. They recognize that, however much confidence they justly have in their own good sense, their interests are better promoted by the merchant than by themselves. They know their lives have not given them the acquired skills that, in a deliberative assembly, are essential even to those of great natural ability. They know merchants have the influence, weight, and superior knowledge to contend with any spirit hostile to manufacturing and trade that might enter public councils. These considerations, and many others, prove what experience confirms: artisans and manufacturers will usually vote for merchants and those they recommend. We must therefore consider merchants as the natural representatives of all these classes.

As for the learned professions, little needs to be said. They form no distinct interest in society. According to their position and talents, they will be the objects of confidence and choice both within their own ranks and from other parts of the community.

What remains is the landed interest. In political terms, especially regarding taxes, I take this to be perfectly united, from the wealthiest landlord down to the poorest tenant. No tax can be laid on land that does not affect the owner of millions of acres as well as the owner of one acre. Every landholder will share a common interest in keeping land taxes low, and common interest is always the strongest bond of sympathy. Even if we suppose a difference in interest between the wealthy landholder and the middling farmer, what reason is there to think the first would be more likely to be elected to the national legislature than the second? If we look at the facts, our own senate and assembly show that moderate landowners predominate in both. This is no less true in the senate, with its smaller numbers, than in the assembly, with its larger ones. Where voter qualifications are the same, whether they choose few or many representatives, votes will go to those they trust most, whether men of large fortunes, moderate property, or no property at all.

It is said that all classes of citizens must have some of their own number in the representative body so their feelings and interests can be better understood and addressed. But we have seen this will never happen under any arrangement that leaves voting free. Where voting is free, the representative body, with too few exceptions to influence the spirit of government, will consist of landholders, merchants, and professionals. Where is the danger that these three groups will not understand or attend to the interests of the different classes? Won't the landholder know what promotes the interest of landed property? And won't his own interest in that property make him resist any attempt to harm or burden it? Won't the merchant understand and want to cultivate the interests of mechanics and manufacturers, since his commerce is so closely tied to them? Won't the professional, neutral toward the rivalries between branches of industry, be likely to act as an impartial judge, ready to promote either side as it serves the general interests of society?

If we consider the temporary moods or attitudes that may prevail in particular parts of society, which a wise administration will never ignore, is the man whose position leads him to extensive inquiry less likely to judge their nature, extent, and basis well than one whose observation does not extend beyond his neighbors and acquaintances? Isn't it natural that a man who is a candidate for the people's favor, and who depends on the votes of his fellow citizens to continue in public office, should inform himself of their dispositions and inclinations and give them their proper weight in his conduct? This dependence, and the necessity of being bound himself, along with his descendants, by the laws he votes for, are the true and strong bonds of sympathy between representative and constituent.

No part of government requires extensive information and a thorough knowledge of political economy more than taxation. The man who best understands these principles will be least likely to resort to oppressive methods or sacrifice any class to raise revenue. It can be shown that the most productive system of finance is always the least burdensome. To exercise the power of taxation wisely, the person holding it must be familiar with the general character, habits, and modes of thinking of the people, and with the resources of the country. This is all that can reasonably be meant by knowing the interests and feelings of the people. In any other sense, the proposition is meaningless or absurd. In that sense, let every thoughtful citizen judge for himself where the necessary qualifications are most likely to be found.
